title: Gamescom Just Became the World's Biggest Gaming Event — and It's Not Feeling the Pressure
summary:
When E3 shut down after the pandemic, the gaming world needed a new home. That home turned out to be Gamescom, the massive trade show held every year in Cologne, Germany. And while you might think the people running it would be sweating under the global spotlight, they insist they're not feeling any pressure at all.

"We don't feel any pressure," Tim Endres, the director of Gamescom at Koelnmesse, told Polygon. "It's quite the opposite: We are happy and excited to see more people from around the world looking at Gamescom."

Gamescom has been around since 2002, when it was called the Games Convention and held in Leipzig. It moved to Cologne in 2009, and since then it's grown every year. Now that E3 is gone, it's the undisputed biggest gaming event on the planet. But the team isn't changing its approach. Stefan Heikhaus, director at the German Games Industry Association, says they feel "a strong responsibility to deliver for the community and the industry every year," but it's "more a level of excitement, not pressure."

This year, Gamescom is adding something huge: Games Done Quick, or GDQ, the world's most famous speedrunning marathon. For the first time ever, GDQ is happening outside North America. From August 28 to 30, players will speedrun games for three days straight, live at Gamescom and streamed on Twitch and YouTube, all to raise money for the charity Gaming for Democracy.

So what's next for Gamescom? Endres says the "ideal future is hard to describe," because the event has evolved so much since his 2009 vision. But one thing is clear: they're not planning a North American expansion. "Our focus is on Cologne as the central meeting point for the global industry and community," Heikhaus said, "supported by our digital formats and our existing international events in Latin America and Asia."

With dozens of games confirmed, including The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt - Songs of the Past and Alien: Isolation 2, Gamescom 2026 is shaping up to be its biggest year yet. And the team behind it? They're just excited to see the world show up.
why_it_matters: Gamescom's new status means the yearly rhythm of game announcements has shifted from the U.S. to Europe, so gamers now look to Cologne for the biggest reveals. It also shows how live events can survive by adding online elements, which changes the way games are marketed and discovered.

background_read: Gamescom is Germany's massive video-game trade show, organized by Koelnmesse (the Cologne-based company that runs the city's exhibition halls) together with the German Games Industry Association, and it began as the Games Convention in Leipzig before moving to Cologne, where it grew into one of the largest public gaming events in the world.
Its rise was helped by the collapse of E3, the longtime Los Angeles gaming expo that once dominated industry announcements, after the pandemic.

Gamescom stays relevant by mixing its physical event in Cologne with digital formats and satellite shows in Latin America and Asia, and this year it is adding Games Done Quick (GDQ), the best-known speedrunning marathon on the internet, in which players complete games as fast as possible while viewers donate to charity.
Moving GDQ outside North America for the first time links Gamescom to an online streaming culture that many younger fans already follow.

perspectives.description: Players win because Gamescom is a huge public show, not a closed industry event, and it gives fans a place to try new games and meet creators. Adding GDQ also brings charity speedrunning to a much bigger stage.

One giant event in one German city can make it harder for smaller regional events to get attention, and fans in North America or poorer regions may feel left out of the in-person side. The focus on Cologne also means the story is told from a European point of view.

Gamescom's growth follows a familiar pattern: when an old anchor collapses, a new one expands to fill the gap. Its shift from Leipzig to Cologne, and from physical-only to hybrid and international formats, mirrors how the gaming market has become more global and online.

The key question is whether Gamescom can stay the main hub as digital showcases continue to grow. If it keeps borrowing internet culture, like GDQ, and expanding into new regions, it could hold that position for a long time.
